title: Good ayis are always on the job: what a domestic-help consultant really sells isn't information
dek: Domestic help is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the hard part of a consultant's job isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale. Both employers and ayis are just pass-throughs for their wages.
why: A frontline post-00s domestic-help consultant lays out an overlooked essential-need industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries. High information density, and the second half is worth more.
who: Dual-income families hiring or about to hire a yuesao or yuer sao; founders and investors watching domestic help and local life services.
skip: From 1:35:37, the segment on the twins family interviewing picture books is more story than substance — fast-forward.

points.h: Good ayis are always on the job
points.body: This market has a circulation paradox: ayis with good reviews never reach the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight to the next one. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could settle on. So the industry's core contradiction is supply — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-help company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

points.h: Every woman in this business has a story
points.body: The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families, giving their time to another household. Two clear traits define why they choose this work: they like children, and they want to earn — not a comfortable life back home farming and drinking tea, but packing everything they own, buying a green-skin train ticket and squeezing into Shanghai.

There has to be a sense of boundaries and proportion between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but people always push for more. More subtly, a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day and may know more about the household's private life than relatives do — the pressure is heavy. Some moms are raising kids effectively widowed, with the dad absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mom company longer; the two become teammates.

points.h: Employers and ayis are both pass-throughs for wages
points.body: For the employer it's like being a pass-through for wages, and the same goes for the ayi: every month the WeChat transfer comes in, and immediately two kids' tuition goes out, then the household living expenses, transferred straight away. Many yuesao and yuer sao earn the most important — sometimes the only — income in their family, which is why their role as wife carries so much weight in the family structure. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background: you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

points.h: How ten pages of job requirements don't scare the ayi off
points.body: The longest yuesao job requirement I've seen ran a full ten pages, at a price that was only the market average. The employer thinks that if every minute is spelled out, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant doesn't forward it directly; she calls first to set the ground: asks about luggage, navigation route, tells her the client says just arrive at this time, then explains that company rules require the employer to list requirements, and she can come to the consultant with any question. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

points.h: Closing the deal is easy; replacing someone is the test
points.body: Yuesao bookings are made in advance; yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi only enters the market once she leaves her previous family, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is available urgently must be bad, when often it's the booked one who's the fake. Closing isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The real difficulty is long-term after-sales — the interview can be thrilling, and afterwards there's a real chance of disappointment. Replacing someone is what truly tests a consultant's level.

points.h: The hardest case requires reading the family's core relationship
points.body: The hardest case: a single mother who is a female executive, wanting a daytime child development companion, but also expecting that person to do housework to cleaning-level standards — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with the assistant, while the core need was shaped by the executive mother. The compromise was cleaners clean, companions companion, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten teaching background; in the end, a sister approaching 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

points.h: Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao depends on age
points.body: In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000 to 16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for newborns, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands depending on age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education, driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the work, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

points.h: Consensus and industry norms are what this trade lacks most
points.body: The live-in norm is that the ayi brings her own personal items and the employer provides big items like bedding, but the two sides haven't formed a consensus. Some think it's lovely when an ayi who's been there a long time grows attached and spends her own wages buying things for the baby; others find it too close. A common situation is a mother who's unhappy that the child is too attached to the ayi. Consultant training teaches this: the person in a family who should be closest to the child is the mom — not the dad, and not the grandparents.

points.h: Young people doing domestic work is long past being a meme
points.body: By the time something becomes a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine. The contraction of the tutoring industry fed a lot of talent into domestic help; child development companions are very young, a cohort in their twenties, because jobs are hard to find and this work includes room and board and covers only one child. After five to eight years of live-in experience, yuying shi and yuesao get older and can't keep up with the kids, so they shift toward training-instructor roles. But whether you do yuying shi or child development companion, planning a three-to-five-year career is very hard.

Because an ayi is a person — people aren't machines, people are in a state where they have emotions.
Closing the deal isn't hard for us — we can always find the employer someone they're happy with, as long as they have a need, right, and a budget. But the hard part usually comes later.
I think right now neither side of the employment relationship has really formed this consensus, hasn't yet accumulated to the point of understanding roughly what state this industry is in.
